runs.text:
A note is a second voice that speaks from the edge of the page.
It does not interrupt the sentence it belongs to; it waits until
the line has ended, then says what the line could not say without
stopping. A reader who ignores it loses nothing of the argument,
and a reader who follows it finds a smaller one running beside it.

The margin is where the two voices agree to live apart. One keeps
the claim moving forward, the other keeps the claim honest, and
neither pretends to be the other. A book that prints its notes at
the end simply walks to the other room for the second voice and
comes back with it under the arm, numbered in the order called.

1. The second voice is older than the argument it serves: the
first printers set it in smaller type so the reader could choose
between the two without losing the thread of either.

2. A note printed at the end keeps the page clean and asks more
of the reader, who must carry the number across the book and back,
the way this document asks you to do right now.
